reason: The runtime's TLS engine offers no OCSP stapling callbacks, no server session cache (resumption is tickets-only and not surfaced), no OpenSSL message trace, no access to the Finished messages or the peer's signature-algorithm list, and no OpenSSL cipher or certificate-compression inventory; the options that would consume those inventories (ciphers, certCompression) are refused as well. tests/diagnostics/compat-absent-tls-engine-members.ts pins the build-time refusals.

SAN DNS/IP matching, the CN fallback, the escaped alt-name form and Node's errors are covered; an IDNA (U-label) hostname is not normalized to its A-label before matching; malformed alt-name text (a trailing comma, an embedded NUL in a name or the host) follows Node's outcomes safely.

The exporter and Node's validation ladder work, including the context argument, the reserved PRF labels a TLS 1.2 connection refuses, and the label ceiling a TLS 1.3 connection applies; the bundled provider caps the derived length at 8160 bytes, where OpenSSL succeeds beyond that.

The TLS 1.2 CLIENT_RANDOM line (on the socket and on the server) matches Node; this TLS provider exports no TLS 1.3 secrets, so a TLS 1.3 handshake emits no key-log lines. A server-level listener runs with `this` = the server, and a plain net or HTTP server keeps a 'keylog' listener inert, as Node's EventEmitter does.

The client session arrives as a Buffer after secureConnect and before 'secure', and is not replayed to listeners added later, as Node's. A TLS 1.2 handshake delivers it once; this TLS provider's server issues a single session, so a TLS 1.3 client sees one event where Node emits one per received ticket (two), and the serialized session is not resumption-capable.

The TLS 1.2 CLIENT_RANDOM line (on the socket and on the server) matches Node; this TLS provider exports no TLS 1.3 secrets, so a TLS 1.3 handshake emits no key-log lines. A server-level listener runs with `this` = the server, and a plain net or HTTP server keeps a 'keylog' listener inert, as Node's EventEmitter does.

A TLS 1.2 client answers the ticket carried by its handshake session (the provider’s own bytes, as any TLS endpoint’s ticket is), and a server socket answers undefined. A TLS 1.3 client answers undefined: this provider does not surface the received ticket in the exported session the ‘session’ event carries, where Node answers a Buffer. Servers mint session tickets as Node’s do.

An established client answers an object and a server-side socket answers null, matching Node's null shapes; the bundled provider does not surface the negotiated group (Node names it — TLSGroup on TLS 1.3, ECDH with the curve and size on TLS 1.2), so a client's object carries no members.

The boolean answer and Node's ladder match: true for an integer in 512..16384, false outside it, and a catchable ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE with Node's text for a fraction, NaN or an infinity. The bundled provider cannot change the record size after the context is set up, so a size is accepted without changing the fragment size (a documented divergence).

The getter answers the server's 48 bytes of ticket key material as a fresh Buffer per call; the setter runs Node's validateBuffer and 48-byte length ladder (ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE, ERR_INTERNAL_ASSERTION) and re-keys the server, so tickets minted under the previous material no longer resume while the tickets it issues do.
